tier_reason: The README states the 1-100x (average 20x, median 12x) speedup over CPython 3.14 across the 80+ programs in examples/ and gives a sieve timing table (CPython 3.10.6 13.4 s, 3.11.0 11.4 s, Shed Skin 0.9.9 1.9 s and 1.8 s), but names no CPU, C++ compiler or flags; the example programs are public but there is no timing harness or per-program result table in the repo, so this is first-party evidence with partial methodology.

corrections.compiler_and_flags: Shed Skin flags --int32 (and --int32 --nowrap --nobounds) for the sieve runs; C++ compiler, version and optimization flags not stated for either measurement (Shed Skin takes its C++ flags from the FLAGS files in its installation, per docs/documentation.md).
corrections.caveats: First-party numbers with no CPU model or compiler version on the page; the examples/ directory has no timing harness or per-program results, so the 1-100x (average 20x, median 12x) figures over CPython 3.14 cannot be checked, and the per-example comparison against CPython 3.10 and PyPy (git tag performance_comparison) is only an image. The sieve table mixes tool versions (CPython 3.10.6/3.11.0, Nuitka 0.6.16, PyPy 3.9 5.8 s, Numba 0.56.4 2.5 s) and the Shed Skin rows used --int32, while Shed Skin now defaults to int64; the README says Numba (int64) would be as fast with 32-bit ints. Only a restricted, implicitly statically typed Python subset compiles, often after substantial refactoring. GPL-3.0 covers the compiler only; the C++ runtime that generated code links is Expat (MIT), with BSD-3-Clause random and BSL-1.0 Boost parts.

notes: Numbers match the README exactly; 6-7x for the sieve is correctly marked as derived (13.4/1.9 = 7.1x vs CPython 3.10.6, 11.4/1.8 = 6.3x vs 3.11.0). Last commit 2026-10-05 (commits.atom), about 1k stars, not archived or a fork, license GPL-3.0-only (compiler) plus Expat runtime as recorded. The asv dashboard (shedskin.github.io/benchmarks) is on a blocked host and was not checked.

tier_reason: doc/site/performance.markdown shows the author's timings against Lua 5.2.3, LuaJIT 2.0.2 -joff, Python 2.7.5/3.3.4 and Ruby 2.0.0, and the harness and per-language benchmark programs are public in test/benchmark, but the page gives no compiler or flags and only '2.3 GHz Intel Core i7' (no CPU model), so first-party with partial methodology.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Method call: wren 0.12 s vs luajit -joff 0.16 s, ruby 0.20 s, lua 0.35 s, python3 0.78 s, python 0.85 s. DeltaBlue: wren 0.13 s vs python3 0.48 s, python 0.57 s (no Lua or Ruby row). Binary trees: luajit -joff 0.11 s, wren 0.22 s, ruby 0.24 s, python 0.37 s, python3 0.38 s, lua 0.52 s. Recursive Fibonacci: luajit -joff 0.10 s, wren 0.20 s, ruby 0.22 s, lua 0.28 s, python 0.51 s, python3 0.57 s. Against Lua 5.2.3 that is about 2.9x, 2.4x and 1.4x faster on method call, binary trees and Fibonacci (derived from page data).
corrections.hardware: MacBook Pro, 2.3 GHz Intel Core i7 (CPU model not named), 16 GB 1,600 MHz DDR3 (author's laptop)
corrections.caveats: Old first-party numbers (undated page; baselines are Lua 5.2.3, LuaJIT 2.0.2, Python 2.7.5/3.3.4 and Ruby 2.0.0, i.e. about 2014) on the author's laptop with no compiler, flags or CPU model stated; modern Lua 5.4, CPython 3.11+ and Ruby 3.x are faster, so the margins are likely smaller today. LuaJIT in interpreter mode (-joff) beats Wren on binary trees (0.11 s vs 0.22 s) and Fibonacci (0.10 s vs 0.20 s); DeltaBlue is compared only with Python. Development is slow: the 2025-11-19 commits are a merged PR (#1194, method-limit checks) plus CI edits, and the previous commits are from 2025-03.

notes: All Wren, Lua, Ruby and Python numbers in the record match the page; the record omitted the LuaJIT -joff rows for method call and Fibonacci, now added. Metadata checked: MIT, 8.1k stars, default branch main, last commit 2025-11-19 (within 12 months, so active), test/benchmark holds matching .wren/.lua/.py/.rb programs.

tier_reason: Upgraded from C: the speed.ruby-lang.org report of 2026-09-20 (source and CSV in github.com/rubybench/yjit-reports, pages branch) times YJIT 4.1.0dev against the CRuby 4.1.0dev interpreter at the same commit (11bb12ad3c) using the public ruby-bench suite pinned at commit 17dcac94 (benchmarks.yml, benchmarks/*), and states the compiler (gcc 14.3.0), configure args and CPU models (Intel Xeon Platinum 8488C, AWS Graviton4).

corrections.baseline: CRuby 4.1.0dev bytecode interpreter (same commit, JIT off); the report also shows CRuby 3.4.7 and YJIT 3.4.7
corrections.workload: ruby-bench (commit 17dcac94) on Ruby master 11bb12ad3c, 2026-09-20: 16 headline benchmarks (activerecord, chunky-png, erubi-rails, hexapdf, liquid-c, liquid-compile, liquid-il, liquid-render, lobsters, mail, psych-load, railsbench, rubocop, ruby-lsp, sequel, shipit) plus about 60 other and micro benchmarks; 5 warmup iterations for the interpreter and 50 for YJIT before timing.
corrections.claimed_speedup: x86_64 (Xeon Platinum 8488C): geomean of the headline benchmarks, YJIT 4.1.0dev is 99.2% faster than CRuby 4.1.0dev and 9.5% faster than YJIT 3.4.7; railsbench 120.1% faster than the interpreter. Per-benchmark interpreter/YJIT time from the x86_64 CSV (derived from page data): activerecord 2.76x, liquid-render 2.89x, railsbench 2.20x, optcarrot 3.79x, lee 1.95x, binarytrees 2.31x, nbody 2.59x, fannkuchredux 4.04x, fib 6.58x, 30k_ifelse 7.62x, 30k_methods 11.84x; 78 of 79 benchmarks faster, knucleotide 0.98x. aarch64 (Graviton4): headline geomean 1.73x, railsbench 1.87x (derived from page data).
corrections.compiler_and_flags: gcc (Ubuntu 14.3.0-12ubuntu1~24~ppa1) 14.3.0; Ruby configured with --disable-install-doc --disable-install-rdoc --enable-yjit --enable-zjit (default optimization flags); YJIT enabled at run time with --yjit; rustc version not stated.
corrections.hardware: x86_64: Intel Xeon Platinum 8488C; aarch64: AWS Graviton4
corrections.caveats: Run by the YJIT team at Shopify (first-party), though code, Ruby commit, build config and CPU are all published and raw per-benchmark CSVs are in rubybench/yjit-reports. Speedups are after warmup (50 YJIT warmup iterations); first-iteration and memory costs differ: YJIT uses more memory than the interpreter on most headline benchmarks (memory chart on the same report). The large micro-benchmark ratios (30k_methods 11.8x, fib 6.6x) do not carry over to applications, where the headline geomean is about 2x on x86_64 and 1.7x on Graviton4. The repository is all of CRuby, so stars and license describe CRuby; YJIT is the yjit/ directory. The VMIL 2021 and MPLR 2023 papers were not opened (dl.acm.org blocked). speed.ruby-lang.org itself was blocked here; its numbers were read from the generated HTML and CSV in rubybench/yjit-reports (branch pages).

notes: The recorded benchmark_url (Shopify/yjit-bench, now ruby/ruby-bench) only carries an explicitly outdated example table whose numbers do match the record, so claimed_speedup and benchmark_url were replaced with the current speed.ruby-lang.org report; the 99.2% geomean was re-derived from the x86_64 CSV (1.99x). Metadata: ruby/ruby 23.8k stars, last commit 2026-10-06, license Ruby or BSD-2-Clause per COPYING (recorded value fine); ruby-bench is MIT.
